concepts.title: Independent pharmacy with prescription delivery and bilingual staff
concepts.rationale: Only 2 pharmacies are mapped in the circle against about 4.9 expected at the benchmark rate for its 23,760 residents, and 36% of households have no vehicle, so getting prescriptions filled is harder for many residents. The 20 rated pharmacies within 2 km average 3.2 stars, which leaves room for a pharmacy that delivers and offers Spanish-speaking staff.
concepts.risk: Insurance contracts and prescription volume are hard to win from Walgreens without an established pharmacy benefit agreement.

concepts.title: Neighborhood bank branch with extended hours and Spanish-language service
concepts.rationale: Five banks are mapped in the circle against about 6.3 expected at the benchmark rate, and the 20 rated banks within 2 km average only 2.9 stars, so residents are underserved on service quality. With a median household income of about $148,732 and 69% of households renting, a branch focused on checking, savings, and rent-deposit accounts with evening hours would meet a broad need.
concepts.risk: Banking is heavily regulated and capital-intensive, and customers tend to stay with the banks where they already hold accounts.

concepts.title: Well-run neighborhood market with fresh produce and fast checkout
concepts.rationale: The circle already has 19 convenience stores, about 0.80 per 1,000 residents against 0.24 at the benchmark, and the 20 rated convenience stores within 2 km average 4.0 stars, so the opening is a better-run store rather than another one. Households with children make up 19% of the circle, and a store with a deep produce section, quick lines, and staff who keep shelves stocked would serve daily family needs better than the current options.
concepts.risk: With so many convenience stores already in the circle, a new store may struggle to win enough repeat trips from shoppers who already have a habit.

docs.text: Google review of Tartine Manufactory (4 out of 5, by Dennis W., 4 months ago): It's a restaurant... It's a bakery... It's a book store... It's a home goods shop.... docs.title: Review of Tartine Manufactory
docs.text:
Google review of Tartine Manufactory (5 out of 5, by Sylwia K, 8 months ago): The sourdough bread at Tartine is the best in the city. Manufactory is their best spot for brunch (other locations are smaller, more cramped and the Sunset one imo as good quality).

Their tartines and sandwiches are pricey but delicious. The tuna, hummus, avocado sandwich is one of the favorites (can easily be shared). The salmon tartine is also solid, especially with a side of avocado. The banana cream pie is also a must!

For dinner, their meatballs and the Margherita pizza are great, easy options.

docs.title: Review of Tartine Manufactory
docs.text: Google review of Tartine Manufactory (4 out of 5, by Chris Brooks, 5 months ago): First time visit for me. Great place for lunch. Very cool ceramics shop and bookstore in same building. We got the kale Caesar salad, breakfast sandwich, tuna melt and banana cream pie. The two standouts were the tuna melt and banana cream pie. Breakfast sandwich though good wasn’t as special. Kale ceasar was delicious. Generous portions. Banana cream pie definitely is an item you would need to share.

docs.title: Review of Tartine Manufactory
docs.text:
Google review of Tartine Manufactory (5 out of 5, by Thomas Reeh, 8 months ago): ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 5 Stars
Tartine Bakery absolutely lives up to the hype. From the moment we walked in, the service was warm, attentive, and genuinely welcoming. The staff was patient, knowledgeable about the menu, and made the whole experience feel relaxed and enjoyable — even during a busy brunch rush.
The standout dish was the soft-cooked scrambled eggs with caviar. Perfectly silky, rich, and buttery, the eggs were cooked to that ideal custardy consistency. The caviar added a beautiful pop of briny flavor that elevated the dish into something truly special. Simple ingredients, executed flawlessly.
Of course, the pastries and bread are phenomenal as always, but the combination of exceptional food and thoughtful service is what really made this visit memorable.
An easy 5 stars — can’t wait to come back. 🌟

docs.title: Review of Foreign Cinema
docs.text:
Google review of Foreign Cinema (5 out of 5, by KB, 3 months ago): Such a fun dinner date night location. The movie makes for an entertaining backdrop and as much as I thought I wouldn’t care about the movie I found myself looking over a fair bit. The courtyard is cozy and intimate with warm patio lights above. Even with the occasional breeze patio heaters keep things toasty.

Service was alright. Our server definitely seemed busy and like maybe we weren’t a priority but the food and atmosphere made up for the small waits.

docs.text: Google review of Grocery Outlet (5 out of 5, by Kristina Hall, 3 months ago): I love this store. It is part of my regular shopping route because these days I’m doing everything I can to keep my grocery prices as low as possible, a no small feat. For example I can buy a pack of approximately 10 chicken thighs for $1.89 a pound. That is enough chicken for my family of two to eat three meals in a week and the package cost approximately $10 so that is six meals for $10 and I can’t think of another protein at this moment that can equal or better that. They have excellent prices on their store brand items, including cheeses, butter, milk, rice, beans, baking staples and so forth. They have very good prices on breads and bagels and eggs. They launched a store brand about a year ago and have been gradually adding products to it, and so the assortment has expanded considerably. Sometimes it’s something as basic as a pound of dried black beans or something more exotic like a jar of tomato based pasta sauce from Italy and it’s companion Italian made dried pasta, which is excellent and very inexpensive. The one thing I would caution about is to take what they claim as a regular store product’s usual price and how much less they’re charging for it with a grain of salt. As an example, a box of Kellogg’s cereal or a pound of Challenge butter. They might post that it is sold at a certain price elsewhere and to show how much less they charge for it. In my experience, however, I find that they often exaggerate how much an item sells for at a different store. And sometimes that exaggeration is quite a bit. Frankly, I wish they wouldn’t do this because it it’s kind of like using that to make them seem like their deal is even better than it already is when it fact, it seems a little bit like trying to pull the wool over our eyes. And it’s unnecessary! What they have, by and large are excellent values. You never know exactly what they’re going to have though many things are there from week to week. Sometimes things are a very good deal because the Best Buy date is coming up fairly soon or they are holiday products that are for a holiday that’s past. It doesn’t mean that the cereal or the candy or the frozen item is any less usable or edible. They also have a large wine and beer selection as well as liquor. They have housewares and some toiletries along with detergent and soda pop. They even have a pretty good selection of pet foods and toys and treats. The Pioneer Building, also known as the Pioneer Trunk Factory - C. A. Malm & Co. building is a historic building in San Francisco, California. The building is located at 2185-2199 Folsom and 3180 18th Streets. It was designed by San Francisco architect Thomas J. Welsh and built in 1902. It was originally two buildings that stood next to each other along 18th street. They were joined into one during rehabilitation in 1985-1986. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1987, as "Pioneer Trunk Factory--C. A. Malm & Co."
The former factory is located just outside the area destroyed by the 1906 fire, and is one of the few remaining examples (e.g.: Levi Strauss & Co. Factory, 250 Valencia Street) of the kind of large completely wooden structure, ornamented with Italianate architectural detail, that was once characteristic of industrial buildings in the Mission district. Its use of Italiente style wooden details resembles many Victorians built in San Francisco at the time. However, the style is unusual for factory buildings, and was perhaps chosen to better fit with the residential buildings that surround it.
The factory originally manufactured trunks for automobiles, which were sold in two stores in downtown San Francisco (before trunks became a standard part of the car.) In addition to the eponymous factory, the building originally also hosted a corner storefront.

docs.text:
Union Race Course was a horse racing track opened in the 1850s in San Francisco, California located in the Mission District. There were two horse race courses in the Mission District at this time, the other being Pioneer Race Course which was located a few blocks away. At the time it was planned to be built, no streets existed in this neighborhood but later it appears to be bound by 19th St to 23rd St and Capp St to Harrison St.
The half mile track was renovated in 1862, moved slightly to softer ground and renamed 'Willows Trotting Park' but the increasing value of the land for housing proved too much. The final horse race was run at Union Race Course on July 18, 1863.
The positioning of this race course, as well as the earlier built race course called Pioneer Race Course appear to have affected the placement of the San Francisco-San Jose Railway. (305 m from the pin.)

The Girls Club in San Francisco, California, also known as Mission Neighborhood Capp St. Center, was built in 1911, in the First Bay Tradition version of Shingle Style architecture. The building was used as a clubhouse for girls and neighborhood center, similar to the Boys Club of America.

It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. According to its NRHP nomination:"The Mission Neighborhood Capp Street Center is significant for the quality of its design and its role in the history of social movements in San Francisco. Built in 1911, the building is an excellent example of the First Bay Tradition. This regional interpretation of the Shingle Style was characterized by the use of shingles and stained wood and picturesque changes in spatial and axial arrangement. Its major practitioners were Ernest Coxhead, Willis Polk, Bernard Maybeck and Julia Morgan. The skillful execution of the design of the Mission Neighborhood Capp Street Center makes it a significant expression of this genre."
The building is a two-and-a-half-story wood-frame structure. The 1911-built building with theatre was expanded by 1923 addition of a gymnasium, making a U-shaped complex.  There is an inner courtyard and a brick alley way.  The main entrance porch is capped with a Georgian-style broken pediment. The upper stories' surface is dark brown shingles. The theatre has small stage, a beamed ceiling and a balcony level. After a fire in the 1940s a sprinkler system was added.

docs.title: Murder of Robert Hillsborough
docs.text:
On June 22, 1977, Robert Hillsborough, a 33-year-old American gay man, was murdered in San Francisco by John Cordova, a 19-year-old from Daly City. Cordova and three other young men followed Hillsborough to his apartment in the Mission and stabbed him fifteen times in the face and chest. 
Cordova was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to 10 years in prison. Though Hillsborough was the nineteenth gay man to be murdered in the United States in 1977, it was his death which galvanized political mobilization amongst the LGBT community to fight for human rights. His family unsuccessfully sued anti-gay activist Anita Bryant for inciting violence against gay people. (519 m from the pin.)

docs.title: The Lexington Club

docs.title: New College of California
docs.text:
New College of California was a college founded in the San Francisco Bay Area in 1971 by former Gonzaga University President John Leary. It ceased operations in early 2008.
New College's main campus was housed in several buildings in the Mission District in San Francisco. The offices at 777 Valencia Street and companion buildings across the street were home to its humanities-based programs, including the Humanities BA, Mathematics, Poetics, Writing and Consciousness, Media Studies, Graduate Psychology, Experimental Performance Institute, Women’s Spirituality MA, Humanities and Leadership, Activism and Social Change, the Teacher Credential Program, as well as a broadcast studio and administration offices. New College of California School of Law was located at 50 Fell Street in the city's Civic Center. The North Bay Campus in Culture, Ecology and Sustainable Community was housed in Santa Rosa, California, in a building owned by the Arlene Francis Foundation, a private foundation run by Peter Gabel, former president of New College and Arlene Francis's son. The Science and Math Institute classes were initially  held at the building at 50 Fell Street then morphed online to become part of the Southern California University of Health Sciences in Whittier, California, within 12 miles (19 km) of downtown Los Angeles. docs.title: Congregation B'nai David
docs.text:
Congregation B'nai David is a former Orthodox Jewish congregation and synagogue, located at 3535 19th Street, in the Mission District of San Francisco, California, in the United States. The synagogue was built in 1908 and abandoned in 1978, due to a decling congregation. This building contained the first northern Californian mikveh, and Orthodox Jews would travel to visit it. Many of the parishioners were immigrants from Poland, Russia, and Romania.
Attendance declined in the 1930s, and regular services ended in the 1960s. The congregation ceased to worship in 1978 and the building was closed. The mikveh was moved to Menorah Square, a Jewish retirement home in Pacific Heights.
Freda Koblick, an artist, purchased the building in 1980 as her art studio and residence. It was later converted into multiple residences.
The building was listed as a San Francisco Designated Landmark on October 5, 1980. (658 m from the pin.)

docs.title: Redstone Building
docs.text:
The Redstone Building, also known as the Redstone Labor Temple (and formerly called "The San Francisco Labor Temple"), was constructed and operated by the San Francisco Labor Council Hall Associates. Initial planning started in 1910, with most construction work done during 1914. Its primary tenant was the San Francisco Labor Council, including 22 labor union offices as well as meeting halls. The building was a hub of union organizing and work activities and a "primary center for the city's historic labor community for over half a century."
The Redstone building played a significant role in the 1917 United Railroads Streetcar Strike as well as the San Francisco maritime strike that led to the 1934 San Francisco General Strike. The Redstone Building has been designated San Francisco's 238th landmark.
The Redstone is located at 2940 16th Street between South Van Ness, formerly Howard Street, and Capp. (679 m from the pin.)

Google review of Costco Pharmacy (1 out of 5, by グドン, a year ago): After more than 3 years of using Costco Pharmacy, I’ve had enough. The only reason we stayed with them was because they’re one of the few places open on Saturdays and close relatively late on weekdays. But their system and inventory management? It’s like they’re stuck in the 1980s.

This week, my doctor prescribed penicillin—a basic, common antibiotic that’s been around since the 1920s—for a severe bacterial infection. I got a text saying my prescription was being prepared, so I waited in the parking lot for almost two hours. When I finally went inside to check, the front desk was dismissive and told me, without a hint of apology, that they were out of stock and I had to go speak to the pharmacist.

The pharmacist couldn’t have been more unhelpful or rude. She didn’t even look at the system before telling me to “just come back tomorrow.” At that point, I had a 104°F fever, could barely swallow, and was visibly in pain. I asked if she could at least check which medication was unavailable—my doctor had prescribed three. If penicillin was in stock, could I please get it for tonight?

Her response? “The more you talk, the slower I get,” followed by telling me her shift was ending soon. I stood there in silence while she reluctantly typed a few things into the system—and just like that, the prescription was suddenly ready. It wasn’t an insurance issue at all—my insurance was perfectly valid. The delay was entirely caused by Costco’s system or process failures.

This isn’t an isolated experience. Just a few days earlier, I waited nearly 90 minutes after getting a “ready” text for my baby’s liquid antibiotics—same disorganization, same cold attitude.

I don’t know if it’s poor management at Costco or just the total collapse of pharmacy care in San Francisco, where Walgreens and CVS are vanishing, and weekend or late-night options are practically nonexistent. But this was infuriating, dehumanizing, and unacceptable.

Google review of Wells Fargo Bank (1 out of 5, by Zamir Films, 6 months ago): I had a very frustrating experience at this Wells Fargo branch (2300 16th St, San Francisco), especially given the circumstances.

This was the day before Easter, and this was one of the only branches open until 2 PM. I went out of my way, burned gas, and rushed there specifically to make it before closing because I had a 3-hour drive ahead of me and wanted to get my checks deposited before the holiday.

I made it on time, waited in a long line, and when I finally got to the front, I was assisted by a young Asian teller named Will Chin.

For context, I regularly deposit larger checks as part of my work. This is normal for me and something I’ve been doing consistently for years without issue.

I fully complied with everything he asked. I attempted my PIN, provided the last four of my Social Security number, and gave him the verification code sent to my phone.

Despite that, there was noticeable hesitation and awkwardness. I observed him and another employee looking at the screen and exchanging looks, then quickly trying to appear more formal when I turned back toward them.

Eventually, he said he needed to verify the checks and took my ID and checks into a back room and closed the door. Another employee asked me to sit down and said it would take about 15 minutes.

I waited, came back up to check, and was told it was still being processed. I sat back down and waited again. By the time they were about to close, he finally came back and told me he couldn’t deposit my checks because they “couldn’t be verified.”

At that point, I started asking questions, and the answers did not add up. When I asked if the checks were flagged, he said no. Then he said it was because of the amount. I asked to see the policy, and he said they do not show policies. Another employee said it was a system issue, not the amount. None of these explanations matched.

I even had the issuer of the checks on the phone at that time, and they confirmed no one from the bank contacted them, despite me being told verification attempts were made.

Then I was told the decision was at the discretion of the teller. That made it clear this was not based on a consistent policy or system flag, but a personal decision.

At one point, I said that as the teller, he is supposed to deposit my checks, and I was told that he did not have to and that it was based on his discretion.

After all that time, I was told I could just use the ATM, which defeats the purpose of coming inside, especially for larger deposits.

Given that depositing larger checks is normal for me, the way this was handled made me feel like I was being treated with unnecessary suspicion instead of as a long-time customer.

I went out of my way, made it before closing, waited in line, complied with everything, and still walked out with nothing handled.

That’s not right.

They exist in a layer just outside the official build of the city, a self-sustaining protocol, running parallel, never fully acknowledged. No matter how early they arrive, the others are already there.

Tommy operates in the same twilight bandwidth. He’s selling a red Giant bike, a small bag with a fresh inner tube, and a scatter of tools that look like they’ve passed through a dozen hands, each leaving behind traces of past transactions, past hustles. The objects feel transient, untethered from their origins, waiting to be assigned new purpose.

“Give me $160,” Tommy says, his voice clipped, efficient, tuned to the rhythms of barter and necessity. “I’ll cut you a deal, throw in all the tools for $170.” The offer isn’t just a number—it’s a shifting node in the market’s low-grade hum, a brief adjustment in the energy web stretched thin over 16th and Mission.

This place isn’t in the city so much as pressed against it, an interface layer where the two realities scrape together, producing sparks, interference patterns. Somewhere in the background, police lights flicker, a brief retinal glitch against the hard gray of the plaza. The system registers their presence but does not pause.

Nothing is truly bought or sold here. Objects change hands, but their gravity remains the same. Tommy will be here until he isn’t. The tamale vendors will be here until they aren’t. The code of the street runs on redundancy. And the city—its real city, the sanctioned, sanitized version—doesn’t notice. Or pretends not to.

Google review of Seventeenth & Noe Market (5 out of 5, by SFglobalnomad, 5 years ago): Nice corner market on a quiet corner in the Castro. They cram a lot into this little store. In the front they have some fresh fruit, an ATM, and lots of liquor. They also have a selection of empanadas which are about $5 each. There is a local cafe two locks away that makes fresh empanadas, so they might want to consider something else.

Staff is friendly. Street parking only, but you could probably double park if you wanted to run in.  Just watch for “street cars”.

docs.title: Review of ABC Market
docs.text: Google review of ABC Market (5 out of 5, by Neal Mueller, 10 months ago): ABC Market on Bryant is a small neighborhood store with consistent operations and a hands on owner who works the primary register. They serve toasted deli sandwiches made to order, and the menu is simple, I get turkey. Sandwiches are toasted on a flat grill and come out fast, usually in under five minutes. The store carries standard groceries, snacks, household items, and a cold case with a strong beer and drink selection that includes major brands, craft options, and nonalcoholic drinks. The décor includes older signage, vintage product displays, and framed memorabilia with a nostalgic layout. The store is clean, well lit, and organized better than any mission corner store

docs.title: Review of Church Street Groceteria
docs.text: Google review of Church Street Groceteria (4 out of 5, by Meg H, 8 years ago): Stopped by this market on a Thursday afternoon around lunchtime for a sandwich - not very busy! There was only one person for both the cash register and deli. The sandwich was pretty decent (I’d definitely eat it again, turkey, havarti, sprouts, avocado, very fresh bread, didn’t care for the sundried tomato) - but I was concerned about the cleanliness... saw the man deal with cash, then come over to the deli and start on my sandwich with bare hands, then accepted my cash. Didn’t see him wash his hands. Would come back for the sandwich but worried about the cleanliness.

docs.title: Review of Church Street Groceteria
docs.text: Google review of Church Street Groceteria (5 out of 5, by Jackie Truong, 5 years ago): Every city needs a corner spot like this with solid deli sandwiches, snacks and the staples. The veggies sandwich is *chefs kiss* loaded with fresh sprouts, sun-dried tomatoes, avo, the works. They also have hummus, falafel (and other vegan friendly goods.) For breakfast sandwiches, stop here too - for my New Yorker friends missing a bodega style menu, this place doesn’t disappoint. Come through!
